newsitem.title: MALDIVES: S.Asian leaders to start summit in Indian Ocean.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian leaders to start summit in Indian Ocean.

text.p: Leaders of seven South Asian nations begin a summit on Monday to breathe new life into their campaign to stimulate economic growth in one of the world's most impoverished regions.

The ninth summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) will focus on ways to speed up growth in member states of the 12-year-old bloc, which represents 1.2 billion people or one fifth of the world's population.

The opening day of the three-day conference was expected to be overshadowed by a meeting between the prime ministers of India and Pakistan, the highest-level talks between the longtime foes in four years.
SAARC foreign ministers acknowledged over the weekend that progress towards economic integration had been slow and agreed to launch a review to revitalise the regional grouping.
"The performance of SAARC has not been as we expected," Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told reporters after the SAARC Council of Ministers meeting on Sunday.
Maldivian Foreign Minister Fathuhulla Jameel said a group of experts would be appointed to "identify measures to revitalise and enhance the effectiveness" of SAARC.

SAARC comprises the Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island nations of the Maldives and Sri Lanka, mostly Hindu India and its Moslem majority neighbours, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

It is a region of stunning geographical, cultural and religious diversity, ranging from the highest point on earth on Mount Everest in Nepal to the fragile Indian Ocean archipelago of this year's host country, the Maldives.

In recent years, SAARC has concentrated on lowering regional trade barriers to try to increase cross-border commerce. But trade among member states still accounts for only three percent of their total world trade.
The region's annual per capita income of $309 is the lowest in the world, and lags behind sub-Saharan Africa's $555, according to the Islamabad-based Human Development Centre.
The rivalry between the region's two biggest states, India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence in 1947, has frustrated SAARC's efforts to pull the region out of poverty.

The first direct talks between Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, set for later on Monday raised hopes that SAARC could eventually ease bilateral tensions that have restrained regional co-operation.
"The overriding factor is that everybody needs SAARC," a Sri Lankan diplomat said on Monday. "The Gujral-Sharif summit would not have been possible if not for SAARC."

At their weekend meeting, SAARC foreign ministers resolved a dispute over a proposed sub-regional group linking Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal, which the Sri Lankan diplomat said demonstrated SAARC's commitment to cooperation.
Pakistan, the Maldives and Sri Lanka had objected to the new "Growth Quadrangle", saying it violated the spirit of SAARC by isolating members.
The foreign ministers decided that some SAARC members could reach sub-regional agreements provided they involved specific projects and other members were kept informed.

Gujral and Sharif were to meet at an island resort in this sun-soaked Indian Ocean archipelago immediately after the inaugural session of the summit. SAARC leaders were to hold a day-long "retreat" on another island on Tuesday and conclude the summit on Wednesday morning.
